clue.text: Politico with cases of kleptomania, megalomania logorrhoea

indicators.note: a case is the outer shell, so only the first and last letter of each following word is kept

parts.note: first and last letters of kleptomania
first and last letters of megalomania
first and last letters of logorrhoea

explanation.surface: A politician accused of a full house of compulsions: stealing, grandiosity and endless talking.
explanation.walkthrough: Kamala Harris, US Vice-President and presidential candidate, is the politico; the three manias are just casings to be stripped.
explanation.definitionFit: Kamala Harris is a prominent American politician, and politico is informal for a person in politics.

clue.text: Money, pure and simple, reportedly area of dispute

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound counts, not the spelling

parts.note: money is cash; pure and simple is mere

explanation.surface: Someone insists that a quarrel is simply about money.
explanation.definitionFit: Kashmir is a Himalayan region whose territory is contested by India, Pakistan and China.

clue.text: Tube in which postmortems, in part, returned

indicators.note: returning means coming back the way you went, so the letters run backwards
only a portion of the long word is taken, a run of its letters

parts.note: a run of letters inside the word

explanation.surface: A tube used during autopsies is sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: Tube is London's Underground railway, not a medical tube.
explanation.definitionFit: A metro is an underground urban railway, which Londoners call the Tube.

clue.text: One taking and playing clarinets

indicators.note: playing a piece freely, so the letters of the instruments are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A musician picks up and plays several clarinets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking' sounds like picking up instruments; it means stealing.
explanation.definitionFit: A larcenist commits larceny, the crime of theft, so is someone who takes property.

clue.text: Do some bonding, embracing one mafia member

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold something in your arms, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: to solder is to bond metal with molten alloy
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone bonds with others by hugging a gangster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bonding' suggests friendship, but it is metalwork joining.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Mafia hierarchy a soldier is a low-ranking made man who carries out orders.

clue.text: Hunk of beef picked up as well: it may be labelled 'B'

parts.note: a side of beef is a large carcass half

indicators.note: picked up means caught by ear, so the sound of the words matters

parts.note: as well means also

explanation.surface: A slab of beef is heard, too, and it carries a B label.
explanation.walkthrough: On vinyl records the second side was labelled B, as in B-side.
explanation.definitionFit: Records and cassettes have side one and side two, the second often marked B on the label.

clue.text: Flier in tailspin: he won't get out alive

indicators.note: a plane in a tailspin is whirling out of control, so the letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pilot in a spinning plane is doomed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a crash; the answer is a prisoner serving a whole-life sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifer is a prisoner sentenced to life imprisonment, who may die behind bars.

clue.text: I lecture, mostly describing how Irvine Welsh writes

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letters are cut

parts.note: India is the radio code word for the letter I
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lecturer explains Irvine Welsh's writing style.
explanation.walkthrough: Irvine Welsh wrote Trainspotting in Edinburgh Scots; I becomes INDIA from the NATO phonetic alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Welsh's novels use phonetic Scottish vernacular, so he writes in a regional dialect rather than standard English.

clue.text: What to shoot in Grand Canyon; on reflection, what to shoot at St. Andrews (photos?)

definitions.text: What to shoot in Grand Canyon

indicators.note: a reflection is a mirror image, so letters appear backwards

parts.words: what to shoot at St. Andrews
parts.note: golfers at St Andrews aim to shoot par
identity cards carry photos

explanation.surface: A tourist guide to shooting: the Grand Canyon's scenery, then golf in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: St Andrews is the Scottish home of golf; IDS is defined by example, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Rafters shoot the rapids, the fast turbulent stretches of the Colorado River in the Grand Canyon.

clue.text: Couple of drinks raised: Grouse?

indicators.note: in a down entry raising lifts the letters so they read from bottom to top

parts.note: two glasses of rum

explanation.surface: Two glasses are lifted in a toast with a shout of the Scotch whisky brand.
explanation.walkthrough: Grouse looks like the whisky Famous Grouse; it is a verb meaning complain.
explanation.definitionFit: To murmur is to grumble quietly, and to grouse is to complain, so both mean muttering discontent.

clue.text: Relax with musical instrument and East End pooch

indicators.note: Cockneys of London's East End famously drop their aitches, so the opening H goes

parts.note: an Indian stringed instrument
a dog

explanation.surface: Chilling out with a sitar and a London mutt.
explanation.definitionFit: To sit around is to idle or laze, a phrasal synonym for relaxing.

clue.text: Sick and tired — in total disarray?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: thoroughly weary of something
second meaning, read as 'eff-ed up', a polite form of a ruder word for wrecked

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second reading: say F-ED UP as 'effed up', the euphemism for something utterly messed up.
explanation.definitionFit: Fed up means weary and exasperated; spelt as the letter F plus ED UP it becomes slang for completely botched.

clue.text: Dalton followed him and Heath east

parts.note: a heath is open moorland
compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone trails a man and the former prime minister Ted Heath eastwards.
explanation.walkthrough: Timothy Dalton followed Roger Moore as James Bond. 'Dalton' and 'Heath' both sound like politicians (Hugh Dalton, Ted Heath), but Heath is just open land.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun stands for the actor Roger Moore, whom Dalton succeeded in the Bond role in 1987.

clue.text: Red meat I'm cooking for Paul's lovely subject

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters before it are mixed into something new

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone cooks red meat as a dish for a friend called Paul.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul McCartney's Beatles song 'Lovely Rita' is about a meter maid; a meter maid is a female traffic warden checking parking meters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Beatles song opens 'Lovely Rita, meter maid', so the parking attendant is the song's subject.

clue.text: Prince is not so thirsty

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Monaco ruler who married Grace Kelly
second meaning: wetter, as weather or ground with more rain is less dry

explanation.walkthrough: Thirsty here means dry, like parched earth; the comparative of rainy is the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Rainier III ruled Monaco; separately, rainier is the comparative adjective of rainy, meaning wetter and less parched.

clue.text: Posted where jouster may be seen

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a knight wears armour of chain links

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is cryptic: a jousting knight appears clad in chain mail.
explanation.definitionFit: Something posted is in transit through the postal system; a knight is likewise dressed in armour made of chain.

clue.text: Big mice to owl, predatory bird

parts.note: OS is short for outsize
mice are what an owl hunts

explanation.surface: Large mice are fair game for an owl, which is a predatory bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The osprey is a fish-eating raptor, a hunting bird of prey.

clue.text: Look up! There's drink all around. You can bank on it!

indicators.note: surrounding on every side, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: a potable is something drinkable

indicators.note: in a down entry up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: lo means look, as in lo and behold

explanation.surface: Someone spots a bar round the room and declares it a dead cert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank on it' looks like a promise; in snooker or pool a bank shot rebounds off a cushion.
explanation.definitionFit: Pool players bank the ball off the cushions of the table, so the table is where banking happens.

clue.text: Stalled in orbit, passing over City of London

indicators.note: to pass over something is to skip it, so those letters are left out

parts.note: in orbit is slang for elated, over the moon
EC is the postcode district of the City of London

explanation.surface: A spacecraft breaks down while orbiting above London's financial district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In orbit' looks like literal spaceflight but means ecstatic; the City's EC postcode is then skipped from its front.
explanation.definitionFit: Static means not moving or progressing, as a stalled thing is at a standstill.

clue.text: Get the latest sauce?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: be brought up to date on news
second meaning: an old variant spelling of ketchup

explanation.walkthrough: Catchup is a less common spelling of ketchup, the tomato sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch up is to get updated on recent news, and catchup is an alternative spelling of the condiment ketchup.

clue.text: Made out like someone with acne?

explanation.walkthrough: 'Made out' tempts as kissing, the teenage sense that sits beside acne; here it means saw.
explanation.definitionFit: To spot is to catch sight of, while spotted also describes skin marked with pimples.

clue.text: Wee fellow loses last of cash, gaining bit of courage to make do

indicators.note: losing one letter while gaining another means a swap of one for the other
gaining brings in a new letter to fill the gap left by the lost one

parts.note: a shrimp is a small person

indicators.note: last of points to the final letter of the next word

parts.note: final letter of cash

indicators.note: a small bit is a single letter, here the opening one

parts.note: first letter of courage

explanation.surface: A small man runs out of money but finds the nerve to get by.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrimp is to economise hard, getting by on very little, which is making do.

clue.text: Upwardly mobile Greek characters tinkled in American trash

indicators.note: moving upward in a down entry means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: xi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
tinkle is a childish word for urinate

explanation.surface: Ambitious Greek folk relieved themselves in rubbish in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upwardly mobile' sounds like social climbing; it reverses the whole string in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep-six is American slang meaning to discard or destroy, from burial at sea in six fathoms.

clue.text: Chat with Italian: 'Like the Beatles?'

parts.note: con is Italian for with
the Beatles were the Fab Four

explanation.surface: Talking with an Italian who asks if you like the Beatles.
explanation.definitionFit: A confab, short for confabulation, is an informal conversation or chat.

clue.text: Domingo, notably, worked as a porter

indicators.note: worked means shaped or kneaded like clay, so the letters that follow are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The tenor Plácido Domingo once had a job carrying luggage.
explanation.definitionFit: Plácido Domingo is a celebrated tenor, an example of a famous singer of the operatic stage.

clue.text: Gus standing up to abandon Leonard in grand display

indicators.note: standing up in a down entry means the name is read bottom to top
abandoning means leaving behind, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: taken as written
the boxer Sugar Ray Leonard

explanation.surface: A man called Gus stands up and walks out on Leonard in a showy display.
explanation.walkthrough: Leonard is the boxer Sugar Ray Leonard, and SUG comes off the front of his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: An array is an impressive arrangement or spread, an imposing show of things.

clue.text: Parts of skunks trimmed for offal

indicators.note: trimming cuts off the edges, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: a skunk's white markings

explanation.surface: Bits of skunk are cut down to make offal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts' suggests cuts of meat in the surface, but it means the stripes on a skunk's fur.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripe is the stomach lining of cattle or sheep, a kind of edible offal.

clue.text: Concepts central to Levant?

indicators.note: central means the core, with the outer letters stripped

parts.note: the Levant is the Mideast, the eastern Mediterranean

explanation.surface: A question whether certain notions are at the heart of Levantine thought.
explanation.walkthrough: Levant must first become MIDEAST, a name for the region, before its middle is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideas are notions or thoughts, which is what concepts are.

clue.text: To detect solar event? Natural ability

indicators.note: detecting here is picking up by ear, so a word is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: a solar flare is a sudden burst of energy from the sun

explanation.surface: A question about spotting something on the sun, then a remark about talent.
explanation.walkthrough: There is a second layer: flair once meant a keen sense of smell, a nose for detecting things.
explanation.definitionFit: Flair is an instinctive talent or knack, an innate gift for doing something well.

clue.text: Mexican chaps invite bridge partners in (separately) for beers

indicators.note: inviting someone in brings them inside, so the pieces go within the other word
separately says the two letters are put in at different places, not together

parts.note: Spanish for men
East and West are partners at the bridge table

explanation.surface: Some Mexican men ask a pair of card players round for drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Homebrews are beers brewed at home rather than bought, so they are beers of a kind.

clue.text: Watson's boss, materialistic chap, is bankrupt

parts.note: Alexander Graham Bell, whose first phone call summoned his assistant Mr Watson
a yuppie, a young upwardly mobile professional

explanation.surface: A detective's superior is a greedy man who has gone broke.
explanation.walkthrough: Watson suggests Sherlock Holmes, but this Watson took the first telephone call from Bell.
explanation.definitionFit: To go belly-up is an idiom for failing financially, like a dead fish floating upside down.

clue.text: Locale of Hardy novels with Elizabeth's favourite

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for with
the Earl of Essex was a favourite of Queen Elizabeth I

explanation.surface: The setting of Thomas Hardy's novels, together with a royal favourite.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy revived the old Anglo-Saxon kingdom's name for his fictional south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hardy set his novels in Wessex, a fictionalised version of Dorset and neighbouring counties.
